prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Willie had a stubborn wart upon his middle toe. Regardless, though, of what he tried the wart refused to go. So Willie went and visited his family foot physician, who instantly agreed it was a stubborn wart condition. The doctor tried to squeeze the wart. He tried to twist and turn it. He tried to scrape and shave the wart. He tried to boil and burn it. He poked it with a pair of tongs. He pulled it with his tweezers. He held it under heat lamps, and he crammed it into freezers. Regrettably these treatments were of very little use. He looked at it and sputtered, “Ach! I cannot get it loose!” “I’ll have to get some bigger tools to help me to dissect it. I’ll need to pound and pummel it, bombard it and inject it.” He whacked it with a hammer, and he yanked it with a wrench. He seared it with a welding torch despite the nasty stench. He drilled it with a power drill. He wrestled it with pliers. He zapped it with a million volts from large electric wires. He blasted it with gamma rays, besieged it with corrosives, assaulted it with dynamite and nuclear explosives. He hit the wart with everything, but when the smoke had cleared, poor Willie’s stubborn wart remained, and Willie’d disappeared.

Here are two elevated ways to polish the text, depending on whether you prefer to keep the rhyming verse format or convert it into sophisticated prose. Both options preserve every detail and plot point of the original story.

### Option 1: Elevated Verse (Rhyming)
*This version retains the original poetic rhythm while elevating the vocabulary and phrasing.*

William was afflicted with an obstinate verruca upon his middle toe,  
And regardless of his earnest efforts, the growth refused to go.  
He consulted his family podiatrist, who promptly did declare  
That a exceptionally stubborn condition was indeed present there.  

The physician sought to squeeze the growth; he strove to twist and turn.  
He endeavored to scrape and shave the mark, to scald it and to burn.  
He probed it with a pair of tongs, pulled gently with his tweezers,  
Exposed the toe to radiant heat, and thrust it into freezers.  

Regrettably, these remedies yielded no tangible defense;  
The doctor sputtered in dismay, "Alas! It will not budge from hence!"  
"I must employ grander implements to aid as I dissect,  
To pound and pummel this affliction, bombard it and inject."  

He struck the site with a heavy hammer, yanked hard with a wrench,  
And seared it with a welding torch despite the pungent stench.  
He bored it with a power drill and grappled it with pliers;  
He zapped it with a million volts from heavy-gauge electric wires.  

He targeted it with gamma rays, besieged it with corrosives,  
And assaulted it with dynamite and nuclear explosives.  
He deployed every measure known, yet when the smoke cleared from the sphere,  
Poor William’s stubborn wart remained—and William had ceased to appear.

---

### Option 2: Eloquent Narrative Prose
*This version transforms the text into a polished, formal storytelling format.*

Young William was afflicted with a remarkably recalcitrant wart upon his middle toe—a growth that steadfastly refused to yield, regardless of his home remedies. Consequently, he sought the counsel of his family podiatrist, who instantly confirmed the exceptionally stubborn nature of the condition. 

The physician embarked on a series of rigorous attempts: he tried squeezing, twisting, scraping, and shaving the growth, followed by efforts to scald and burn it. He probed the site with tongs, tugged with tweezers, subjected it to intense heat lamps, and plunged it into deep freezers. Regrettably, these interventions proved to be of very little utility. Dismayed by the lack of progress, the doctor sputtered, “Alas! I cannot detach it!” 

Determined to prevail, he declared the need for larger implements to dissect, pummel, bombard, and inject the lesion. What followed was a dramatic escalation: he struck the wart with a hammer, yanked it with a wrench, and seared it with a welding torch, oblivious to the foul stench. He proceeded to bore into it with a power drill, grapple with pliers, and surge one million volts of electricity through heavy wiring. Finally, he deployed gamma radiation, inundated the site with corrosive agents, and assaulted it with both dynamite and nuclear explosives. 

Having leveled every conceivable force against the affliction, the doctor waited. Yet, as the smoke gradually cleared, a tragic irony emerged: William’s stubborn wart remained entirely intact, while poor William himself had completely vanished.

outputs.L3:
After weeks of trying every over-the-counter cream, pumice stone, and old wives' remedy to no avail, Willie finally admitted defeat. The small, surprisingly stubborn wart on his middle toe refused to budge. Frustrated and out of options, he scheduled an appointment with a local foot physician, confident that a professional touch would quickly solve the minor inconvenience.

At first, the doctor approached the problem with routine medical confidence. He began with standard, non-invasive protocols, applying high-potency chemical ointments and attempting to freeze the growth using liquid nitrogen. When cryotherapy yielded no results, he shifted to physical techniques, carefully using a sterile scalpel and curette to cut and scrape the stubborn tissue away. Yet, to the physician's growing disbelief, all conventional methods proved utterly unsuccessful. The wart remained stubbornly intact, completely impervious to the tools of modern medicine.

Determined not to be outsmarted by a minor skin affliction, the doctor’s professional composure vanished, replaced by an aggressive, mechanical approach. He abandoned his traditional medical equipment in favor of heavy industrial tools. First, he attempted to loosen the growth with precise blows from a ball-peen hammer, followed quickly by the high-pitched whine of a power drill. When those failed to make an impression, he put on a safety visor, sparked a welding torch, and blasted the toe with intense heat, before finally running thousands of volts of electricity directly through Willie's foot. 

By this point, all logic and medical ethics had been completely tossed aside in favor of pure obsession. Seeing that industrial force had failed, the doctor escalated to apocalyptic hazards. He wheeled in a heavy cannon to bombard Willie's toe with lethal doses of gamma rays. Still unsatisfied, he strapped a stick of dynamite directly to the digit and lit the fuse. Finally, driven to absolute madness by the invincible growth, the doctor resorted to the ultimate measure: detonating a tactical nuclear explosive right inside the examination room.

A deafening silence eventually settled over the smoldering, radioactive crater where the clinic had once stood. As the thick mushroom cloud of smoke slowly cleared, a solitary, bizarre sight emerged from the rubble. Sitting atop a pile of ash was the wart, completely unharmed and untouched by the immense destruction. Willie, on the other hand, had completely disappeared without a trace.
outputs.L4:
It began as a minor inconvenience: a pale, unassuming speck resting upon the knuckle of Willie’s left middle toe. It did not throb, nor did it bleed, but it was an unwelcome intruder nonetheless. Seeking a swift and professional resolution, Willie booked an appointment with Dr. Ignatius Krell, a podiatrist whose polished brass doorplate proudly proclaimed a hundred-percent success rate in the eradication of cutaneous anomalies.

"A simple Verruca vulgaris," Dr. Krell declared, peering through a lighted magnifying glass. "A week of salicylic acid, a brief freeze, and you’ll be dancing the waltz."

The acid, however, did nothing but turn the surrounding skin a gentle pink. Undeterred, Dr. Krell brought out the liquid nitrogen. With a quiet hiss, he blasted the growth at three hundred degrees below zero. Ice crystals blossomed across Willie’s toe, but when the frost thawed, the wart remained—not merely unscathed, but seemingly hydrated by the experience.

"Fascinating," Dr. Krell muttered, his eyes narrowing. "An intransigent specimen. We must abandon gentle persuasion."

By the third week, the podiatrist’s cozy office had shed its calming ambiance. Dr. Krell bypassed the scalpel and produced a high-speed carbide Dremel tool. The drill whined at thirty thousand RPMs as it struck the growth. Sparks flew, fillagrees of bone-dust filled the air, and the bit shattered into three pieces. The wart did not possess so much as a scratch; if anything, its textured surface seemed to mock the physician. 

Desperate to maintain his flawless track record, Dr. Krell’s methodology devolved from medical practice into industrial assault. He dragged Willie into a lead-lined basement laboratory equipped with heavy machinery. First came the thermal lance, which melted Willie’s leather boot into a foul-smelling slag while the wart glowed with a comfortable, warm radiance. Next came the high-voltage electrical apparatus. Dr. Krell clamped copper leads directly to Willie’s ankle and toe, channeling fifty thousand volts of raw grid power through the appendage. 

The shock sent Willie into violent convulsions, singeing off his eyebrows, carbonizing his socks, and rendering his left leg temporarily paralyzed. When the smoke cleared, the wart sat atop the blackened, blistered toe, pink and pristine, looking very much like a well-tended orchid in a burnt forest.

"It is an insult to science!" Dr. Krell shrieked, his hair standing on end, his coat stained with soot. "It is a personal affront to my pedigree!"

Willie, weak, trembling, and severely traumatized, feebly suggested that perhaps he could just live with the wart. "I can just wear wider shoes, Doctor..." he rasped.

"Silence!" bellowed Dr. Krell. "We do not compromise with dermatological defiance!"

Reason had long since abandoned the operation. Exercising questionable military connections and liquidating his life savings, Dr. Krell secured a experimental, micro-tactical thermonuclear warhead. He transported a half-dead Willie to a classified testing facility deep within the Nevada desert. 

Strapped to a steel gurney in the epicenter of a massive blast crater, Willie could only watch through bleary eyes as Dr. Krell retreated to a reinforced concrete bunker two miles away. The miniature atomic charge was wired directly to the middle toe of Willie's left foot. 

Over the intercom, Dr. Krell’s voice crackled, manic and triumphant. "Let us see how your cellular matrix holds up to the temperature of the sun, you miserable bump!"

The countdown reached zero. 

A blinding, apocalyptic flash illuminated the desert, followed by a seismic shockwave that shook the earth for miles. A column of fire and radioactive dust surged into the heavens, vaporizing the gurney, the ground beneath it, and every atom of Willie’s physical form. Millions of degrees of heat rendered the surrounding sand into a smooth, cratered basin of emerald glass.

Hours later, clad in a heavy radiation suit, Dr. Krell Geiger-countered his way into the smoking crater to survey his victory. He knelt down at ground zero, sweeping away a layer of hot ash. 

There, resting in the exact center of the fused glass, was no trace of Willie. His body, his clothes, and his bones had been completely annihilated, converted into floating atmospheric drift. But hovering serenely atop a tiny mound of irradiated dust was the wart. It was entirely unharmed, perfectly intact, and seemingly nourished by the gamma radiation.

Dr. Krell fell to his knees, staring in horror at the immortal growth. 

In his monomaniacal quest to destroy a trivial nuisance, he had incinerated the very patient he had sworn to heal. The crater stood as a silent, terrifying monument to human hubris—a stark reminder of the catastrophic folly of wielding remedies vastly more destructive than the afflictions they are meant to cure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a funny, rhyming poem in the style of Shel Silverstein about a boy named Willie who visits a doctor to get rid of a stubborn wart on his toe.
counterfactuals.output:
Little Willie had a wart
Upon his pinky toe.
It was lumpy, green, and stubborn,
And it simply wouldn't go.
He tried rubbing it with peanut sauce,
He soaked it in hot tea,
Then he marched into the office
Of Old Doctor Barnaby.

The doctor put his glasses on
And gave a heavy sigh.
"A silly little bump," said he,
"Will vanish in an eye!"
He sprayed it with an icy frost—
*A CRUNCH-Y-FREEZY-BLAST!*
The wart just put a sweater on
And said, "Well, that went fast!"

The doctor brought a pair of pliers,
A jackhammer, a drill,
A bowl of boiling vinegar,
A giant purple pill.
He used a shiny laser beam,
A stick of dynamite,
He even asked politely,
"Could you leave my sight tonight?"

The wart just yawned and stretched a bit,
And sang a happy song:
"I love it here on Willie's toe,
It's where I best belong!
The sock is warm, the sweat is fresh,
The rent is totally free!
You'll never, ever pry me off
This cozy pinky-tee!"

Then Doctor Barnaby grew mad,
And yelled, "ENOUGH OF THAT!"
He grabbed a pair of garden shears,
A plunger, and a bat.
He gave a yank, he gave a twist,
He pulled with all his might—
And with a giant *SQUISH-Y-POP!*
The wart flew out of sight!

Hooray! The stubborn wart was gone!
Young Willie cheered with glee!
"My toe is saved! My foot is fine!
Oh, thank you, Barnaby!"

...Except the wart had landed *SPLAT!*
Right on the Doctor's nose,
And now it's building balconies
And wearing fancy clothes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous poem about a doctor who escalates from normal medical tools to power tools, electricity, and explosives just to treat a minor condition. It should end with a dark twist.
counterfactuals.output:
Young Billy had a problem that was very small and mild:
A microscopic splinter in the finger of the child.
Dr. Evans donned his glasses, took a breath, and checked the speck,
And muttered, "Do not fear, my boy, I’ll fix this in a sec."

He started off with tweezers, but the splinter wouldn't yield.
"A stubborn piece of oak!" he cried. "We must expand the field!"
He set aside the cotton swabs and fetched a power drill,
Then revved a gas-powered chainsaw to test his medical skill.

*Vroom-vroom!* went the chainsaw as it chewed through flesh and bone,
While Billy could do nothing but hysterically groan.
"It’s deeper!" yelled the doctor as he grabbed an angle grinder,
"This sliver's dodging surgery, but I am gonna find her!"

The grinder showered sparks across the bloody, ruined room,
"We need more force!" the doctor screamed, embracing utter doom.
He dragged in heavy cables from the city’s power grid,
"A million volts of shock should loosen up the little kid!"

*ZAP!* Blue lightning crackled as he slapped the cables down,
Extinguishing the streetlights and the power to the town.
Poor Billy’s frame was smoking, and his socks were turned to rust,
While half the operating room was sizzled into dust.

"STILL STUCK!" roared Dr. Evans, now maniacally unhinged,
"It’s time for raw explosives!" as his eyebrows were completely singed.
He packed ten sticks of dynamite, a belt of C4 plastic,
And rigged a military bomb—unregistered and drastic.

He slapped on safety goggles, yelled, "STAND BACK! DO NOT IGNORE!"
And pressed the bright red detonator button on the floor.

***KABOOM!*** 

The whole facility shattered, the roof was blown away,
A giant mushroom cloud turned afternoon to dark and gray.
A two-mile-wide disaster zone was all that now remained,
Where rubble burned and toxic ash endlessly rained.

The doctor rose up from the dust, wiped soot off from his smock,
And poked around the crater in a state of joyous shock.
He found a speck of carbonized, obliterated wood:
"The splinter's gone! The cure worked just as I predicted it would!"

He turned toward the trembling crowd who watched in horrified defeat,
And pointed at a little girl weeping on the street.
He brandished a rocket launcher, with a wide, unblinking grin:
"Next patient! You've a hiccup? Excellent—step right in!"
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a silly story in verse about a toe wart that refuses to disappear?
counterfactuals.output:
Upon the digit of my shoe,
A tiny bump began to brew.
Right on the tip of my big toe,
A little squatter started to grow.

I named him Barnaby the Wart,
Who treated foot care like a sport.
He built a porch, he poured some tea,
And chuckled, "You’re stuck here with me!"

I bought a patch of acid gel,
To send him to the depths of hell.
I wrapped it tight and went to sleep,
Expecting him to melt and weep.

I pulled it off at dawn’s first light—
He had a tan! He looked so bright!
He waved his little bumpy hands
And said, "I love these spa-day bands!"

So next, I brought out silver tape,
To smother him and change his shape.
I bound my foot for seven days,
Denied him air and solar rays.

Unwrapped the gray, peeled back the skin...
He put a tiny crown upon his chin!
"A suffocating blanket coat!
You are the best," he squeaked out loud.

I ran to see a doctor friend,
To bring this nightmare to an end.
The doctor smiled and brought the chill:
A blast of frost to make him still.

He sprayed the gas, icy and blue,
And froze the toe right through and through!
I gasped in pain, I winced, I cried—
While Barnaby just went inside,

And put a winter beanie on!
I thawed my foot—he wasn't gone!
He sang a song of ice and snow,
And did a jig upon my toe.

I tried a peel from a banana,
I sang a spell in weird soprano,
I rubbed him down with pumice stones,
I begged him with desperate moans.

I soaked in juice of lemon lime,
I covered him in sacred thyme.
But Barnaby just grew a smile,
And said, "I think I'll stay a while!"

So now we walk, just him and me,
In bumpy, odd fraternity.
I buy my socks a size too wide,
To keep my little friend inside.

And if you see me limp a bit,
It’s just because my shoe don't fit—
Or maybe Barnaby is throwing
A party where my toe is growing!
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem about a stubborn wart.
counterfactuals.output:
Upon my thumb, a little mound,
The toughest bump that could be found.
Uninvited, rough, and gray,
It moved right in and chose to stay.

I bought a gel, I tried a cream,
To wake me from this bumpy dream.
I poured on acid, dripped it thick,
And hoped the stuff would do the trick.

I wrapped it up in silver tape,
Allowing no air to escape.
I blasted it with icy spray,
And yelled, "It's time you go away!"

The frost thawed out, the tape came loose,
It laughed at every clever ruse.
It nestled deeper in my skin,
Determined that it's going to win.

It braves the doctor, scorns the chill,
And sits upon my knuckle still.
I guess we’re stuck forevermore—
Me and the bump I so abhor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a dark comedic poem with a lighthearted cadence. Plot: A foot physician tries everything from heat lamps to nuclear weapons to destroy Willie's wart, but accidentally obliterates Willie while the wart survives.
counterfactuals.output:
Poor Willie had a tiny bump, a monster on his toe,  
A stubborn little plantar wart that simply wouldn’t go.  
He saw Dr. Bartholomew, a foot-physician bold,  
Who swore he’d kill the hideous thing before the day grew cold.  

He painted it with acid drops, he froze it till it cried,  
He scraped it with a scalpel, but the stubborn bump survived.  
In fact, it seemed to giggle as it swelled a tiny bit,  
So Doc brought out a blowtorch for a sizzle-roasting fit!  

He cranked the heavy heat lamps up to ninety-thousand degrees,  
He pulled out an angle grinder and brought Willie to his knees.  
Young Willie hollered, "Doctor, wait! I’m losing half my skin!"  
"Hush up!" spat the physician, "This is where the fun begins!"  

He strapped a laser to the foot, designed for deep space mining,  
He brought a pneumatic jackhammer while poor old Will was whining.  
He packed the toe with dynamite and pulled the blasting pin—  
*KABOOM!* The clinic walls caved out, the ceiling caved right in!  

The doctor coughed through heavy smoke and wiped his bloodied brow,  
"A tricky beast," the doctor sneered, "but I will get it now!"  
He ordered up a missile from a military strike,  
A mega-tonner warhead of the thermonuclear type.  

He aimed the payload at the foot, strapped Willie to the floor,  
And pressed the big red button with a triumphant roar!  
A blinding flash! A sonic boom! A booming mushroom cloud!  
A thousand square miles flattened in a dusty, atomic shroud!  

And when the fallout settled down, poor Willie was no more—  
Vaporized to drifting dust upon the crater floor.  
No bone was left, no drop of blood, no sign of shoe or sock,  
Just silence in the scorched abyss upon a glowing rock.  

And right there in the center, looking victorious and bright,  
Sat Willie’s wart—without a scratch—and throbbing in the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
